critic.assessment:
Coverage check: all 58 production contracts under contracts/ (excluding contracts/test) are covered by at least one lens's reviewed list. The handful not named verbatim (contracts/interfaces/Enum.sol, ERC1155TokenReceiver.sol, ERC721TokenReceiver.sol, ERC777TokensRecipient.sol, IERC165.sol, INativeCurrencyPaymentFallback.sol, external/SafeMath.sol, examples/guards/BaseGuard.sol, handler/extensible/TokenCallbacks.sol, common/NativeCurrencyPaymentFallback.sol) were read as dependencies by the guards, handlers, gas-refund, managers and libraries lenses. No production file is unreviewed.

Attack classes I checked myself and ruled out (with evidence): (1) Selector collisions in the dispatch chain: computed every function selector from build/artifacts for Safe (31), SafeL2 (31), ISafe, CompatibilityFallbackHandler (12), ExtensibleFallbackHandler (13), TokenCallbackHandler, SafeProxy, factory and libraries; no Safe x handler overlap, nothing shadows SafeProxy.masterCopy() 0xa619486e, every ISafe selector is implemented by Safe (only the two legacy msg.sender overloads are outside ISafe, by design), and no clash with common ERC-20/721/1155/777, ERC-1271, ERC-4337, proxy or guard selectors. (2) ERC-165 misreporting: TokenCallbackHandler.supportsInterface (contracts/handler/TokenCallbackHandler.sol:60-65) reports exactly 1155/721/165; ExtensibleFallbackHandler._supportsInterface (contracts/handler/ExtensibleFallbackHandler.sol:20-28) adds ERC1271, muxer, ERC165Handler, IFallbackHandler -- all actually implemented. (3) Token callbacks as phishing vectors: callbacks are view/pure and only make the Safe accept tokens; no state or auth effect (handlers lens #14 confirmed). (4) Storage slot collisions: managers lens #9 verified the three keccak slots and the sequential layout; ExtensibleBase/ReentrancyTransactionGuard state lives in the handler/guard contracts, not the Safe. (5) ERC-4337: only contracts/test/Test4337ModuleAndHandler.sol (explicitly DO NOT USE) exists; README.md:27-39 describes an opt-in live-bundler test; no production 4337 surface in this repo. (6) EIP-7702 delegation to the singleton: F02 plus managers #12-13 and proxy #8-9/#16 cover initialization, self-ownership, authorized-bypass and re-delegation; no further concrete hypothesis. (7) zkSync/EraVM remnants: hardhat.config.ts:134-137 is a plain EVM RPC network entry with no zksolc settings; CHANGELOG.md:69-73 documents EraVM deprecation and that EraVM Safes cannot upgrade; no production code remnants. (8) Gas-limit DoS in getters: OwnerManager.getOwners (contracts/base/OwnerManager.sol:174-186) is an O(ownerCount) view; getModulesPaginated page size is caller-chosen; no on-chain consumer loops over owners. (9) Safe/SafeL2 event parity: SafeL2.onBeforeExecTransaction is invoked at contracts/Safe.sol:150 before nonce++ at :168 and encodes the pre-increment nonce (contracts/SafeL2.sol:74); both execTransactionFromModule and execTransactionFromModuleReturnData share preModuleExecution (contracts/base/ModuleManager.sol:113) so the module event is emitted identically. (10) ErrorMessage: all 33 revertWithError literals are exactly 5 bytes. (11) secp256r1 CI coverage: package.json:20-24 runs test:secp256r1 (HARDHAT_SECP256R1_PRECOMPILE=1) as part of npm run test, which the CI tests job executes.

Three new facts surfaced that the lenses either got wrong or did not examine, and they drive the gaps below: (a) Empirically (hardhat script against the committed 0.7.6 artifacts) Safe.execTransaction with operation = 2 or 255 is NOT rejected at ABI decoding -- it proceeds to GS020, i.e. the legacy ABI coder v1 does not range-check Enum.Operation, contradicting the assembly-memory lens (#1) and libraries lens (#9); 0.8.x builds (ABI coder v2) would Panic(0x21) instead, and CI runs only benchmark/*.ts under 0.8.24 (.github/workflows/ci.yml:63-73, package.json:27), so the test suite never exercises the 0.8 build. (b) contracts/handler/CompatibilityFallbackHandler.sol:11 states the handler "Provides compatibility between pre 1.3.0 and 1.3.0+ Safe" while isValidSignature (:83) calls checkSignatures(address,bytes32,bytes), which only exists in Safe >= 1.5.0; FallbackManager.setFallbackHandler has no version check. (c) certora/specs/Signatures.spec:16 summarizes Safe.checkContractSignature as NONDET and :17 summarizes p256Verify as CONSTANT, so the post-audit #1115 SecuredSignatureValidator path is entirely outside the formal verification that CI runs. Overall the codebase remains well covered; the remaining gaps are expected to yield low/informational findings with documentation or test-coverage remediation rather than exploitable issues.

findings.title: 1.5.0 CompatibilityFallbackHandler / ExtensibleFallbackHandler cannot verify ERC-1271 signatures on 1.3.0 / 1.4.1 Safes despite NatSpec compatibility claims; no version guard or documentation
findings.description: contracts/handler/CompatibilityFallbackHandler.sol:11 states the handler 'Provides compatibility between pre 1.3.0 and 1.3.0+ Safe smart account contracts', and contracts/handler/ExtensibleFallbackHandler.sol:12 states 'Designed to be used with Safe >= 1.3.0'. Both handlers' ERC-1271 path, however, calls `safe.checkSignatures(address(0), messageHash, _signature)` (CompatibilityFallbackHandler.sol:83; SignatureVerifierMuxer.sol:168), i.e. selector 0xf855438b `checkSignatures(address,bytes32,bytes)`, which only exists in Safe 1.5.0 (contracts/Safe.sol:301). A selector scan of the shipped bytecode in test/json/safeDeployment.json confirms that safe130, safe130l2, safe141 and safe141l2 dispatch only the legacy 0x934f3a11 `checkSignatures(bytes32,bytes,bytes)`. On an older Safe the unknown selector re-enters FallbackManager.fallback (contracts/base/FallbackManager.sol:55-87), which forwards it back into the same handler: CompatibilityFallbackHandler has no such function and no fallback, so it reverts with empty data; ExtensibleFallbackHandler's catch-all fallback reverts with 'method handler not set' (contracts/handler/extensible/FallbackHandler.sol:33-35). FallbackManager.setFallbackHandler (FallbackManager.sol:46-49) performs no version check, the handlers are shared deterministic singletons (src/deploy/deploy_handlers.ts), and neither CHANGELOG.md (lines 105-149) nor docs/overview.md (fallback-handler section, lines 141-157) mentions a minimum Safe version. Empirical matrix (hardhat, shipped 1.3.0/1.3.0L2/1.4.1/1.4.1L2 bytecode x {CFH 1.4.1, CFH 1.5.0, EFH 1.5.0}): with CFH 1.5.0 on any pre-1.5.0 Safe the empty-signature (signedMessages) path still returns 0x1626ba7e, but ECDSA and contract-signature paths revert with empty data, and the legacy `isValidSignature(bytes,bytes)` (0x20c13b0b) also reverts (removed in 1.5.0); getMessageHash, getMessageHashForSafe, getModules, simulate, encodeTransactionData, token callbacks and supportsInterface all keep working and return correct data (no silent wrong data). With EFH 1.5.0 on a pre-1.5.0 Safe the result is the same for signatures (reverts 'method handler not set'). With CFH 1.4.1 on a 1.5.0 Safe everything works through the legacy overload at Safe.sol:439-442 (see ruled_out for the executor analysis), except encodeTransactionData (see separate finding). Operational: an ordinary owner-signed `setFallbackHandler(CFH_1.5.0)` on an un-migrated 1.3.0/1.4.1 Safe (the normal 'update fallback handler' flow, and the obvious thing to do for a wallet that lists the latest deterministic handler address) silently disables all signature-based ERC-1271 verification for every dApp until reverted; restoring CFH 1.4.1 or running SafeMigration.migrateSingleton/migrateWithFallbackHandler re-enables it. The behaviour fails closed (no signature is wrongly accepted), which is why severity is low.
findings.attack_path: Self-inflicted misconfiguration, not an external attack: Safe owners of a 1.3.0/1.4.1 Safe execute setFallbackHandler(<1.5.0 CompatibilityFallbackHandler or ExtensibleFallbackHandler>) without migrating the singleton (or a wallet/UI offers 'latest handler' without a version check). Afterwards every dApp call `safe.isValidSignature(bytes32,bytes)` with a non-empty signature reverts with empty return data (CFH) or 'method handler not set' (EFH): off-chain signing (Permit2, CoW, Seaport, SIWE, etc.) stops working, and because the revert data is empty the failure is hard to diagnose. The same happens if a 1.3.0/1.4.1 Safe with the 1.5.0 CFH is used as a contract-signer owner of another Safe (outer 1.5.0 Safe returns GS024). Reproduced with a temporary hardhat spec (deleted) using test/json/safeDeployment.json bytecode and the deployed 1.5.0 handlers.
findings.evidence: CompatibilityFallbackHandler.sol:11 '@notice Provides compatibility between pre 1.3.0 and 1.3.0+ Safe smart account contracts.'; :83 `safe.checkSignatures(address(0), messageHash, _signature);`. ExtensibleFallbackHandler.sol:12 '@dev Designed to be used with Safe >= 1.3.0.'; SignatureVerifierMuxer.sol:168 `safe.checkSignatures(address(0), messageHash, signature);`. Safe.sol:301 `function checkSignatures(address executor, bytes32 dataHash, bytes memory signatures) public view override` (new in 1.5.0, introduced by #866 e9a58ce which replaced `safe.checkSignatures(messageHash, messageData, _signature)` in both handlers). FallbackManager.sol:46-49 setFallbackHandler has only the `handler == address(this)` check (GS400). Bytecode selector scan: safe130/safe130l2/safe141/safe141l2 contain 0x934f3a11 but not 0xf855438b; compatibilityFallbackHandler141 contains 0x934f3a11, 0x1626ba7e and 0x20c13b0b. Test output: 'Safe 1.4.1 + handler CFH150: emptySig OK:0x1626ba7e..., ecdsa REVERT(empty), contractSig REVERT(empty), legacyIsValidSig REVERT(empty), getMessageHash OK(correct), getModules OK(correct), encodeTransactionData OK(correct), simulate OK(correct)'; 'Safe 1.3.0 + handler EFH150: ecdsa REVERT("method handler not set")'; '1.4.1 after setFallbackHandler(CFH150), unmigrated: REVERT(empty)'; '1.4.1 after restoring CFH141: OK'; '1.4.1 after migrateSingleton (CFH141 retained): OK'; '1.4.1 migrateWithFallbackHandler -> OK'.
findings.recommendation: 1) Correct the NatSpec: CompatibilityFallbackHandler.sol:11 should state that the handler requires Safe >= 1.5.0 (it provides compatibility for *callers* that expect pre-1.5.0 Safe methods, not compatibility with pre-1.5.0 Safe singletons); likewise ExtensibleFallbackHandler.sol:12 should say Safe >= 1.5.0. 2) Add a 'minimum Safe version' note for each handler in CHANGELOG.md (Current version section, near lines 105-111 and 131-138) and docs/overview.md (fallback-handler section), and in the SafeMigration NatSpec state that 1.5.0 handlers must only be set after the singleton is migrated. 3) Optionally make the handler fail loudly instead of with empty data: in isValidSignature, call the Safe via a low-level staticcall and revert with a descriptive reason (e.g. 'GS0xx: handler requires Safe >= 1.5.0') when the call returns empty revert data, or fall back to the legacy `checkSignatures(bytes32,bytes,bytes)` overload only if that is judged acceptable (note it reintroduces msg.sender-based pre-approval semantics the #866 change deliberately removed, so a plain revert with a clear reason is the safer option). 4) Add a regression test in test/handlers that installs the 1.5.0 handlers on the shipped 1.3.0/1.4.1 bytecode and asserts the documented behaviour.

findings.title: A 1.5.0 Safe using the 1.5.0 CompatibilityFallbackHandler can no longer act as a contract-signer owner of a 1.3.0 / 1.4.1 Safe (legacy isValidSignature(bytes,bytes) removed); undocumented nested-Safe upgrade hazard that migrateWithFallbackHandler triggers and migrateSingleton avoids
findings.description: Safe 1.3.0 and 1.4.1 verify contract signatures (v == 0) by calling the owner's legacy `isValidSignature(bytes data, bytes signature)` (selector 0x20c13b0b) with the message pre-image. The 1.5.0 CompatibilityFallbackHandler implements only `isValidSignature(bytes32,bytes)` (CompatibilityFallbackHandler.sol:73); CHANGELOG.md:111 records that 'the legacy function was removed from the compatibility fallback handler contract' but no document states the consequence: a 1.5.0 Safe equipped with the 1.5.0 handler (any freshly deployed 1.5.0 Safe, or a Safe migrated via SafeMigration.migrateWithFallbackHandler, SafeMigration.sol:80-83) cannot produce a valid contract signature for an un-migrated parent Safe or for any other consumer that still uses the legacy ERC-1271 selector. The legacy Safes bubble the handler's revert verbatim, so the parent's execTransaction fails with empty revert data. By contrast SafeMigration.migrateSingleton (SafeMigration.sol:71-74) keeps the 1.4.1 handler, which implements both selectors, so that path preserves the nested signer role. Empirically: outer 1.3.0/1.4.1 Safe with owner = 1.5.0 Safe+CFH 1.5.0: execTransaction with a contract signature -> REVERT(empty) under both inner hash conventions; with owner = 1.5.0 Safe+CFH 1.4.1 -> OK (inner signs over the pre-image). The parent is not bricked: the child can call parent.approveHash(txHash) as msg.sender (an owner) and a v == 1 signature then executes (verified), after which the parent can be migrated. Nothing in CHANGELOG.md, docs/signatures.md or SafeMigration's NatSpec warns operators of nested Safes to upgrade the parent before (or instead of) upgrading the child with the fallback-handler update. Fails closed; low severity.
findings.attack_path: Operational, not adversarial: an organisation with a nested setup (parent Safe 1.4.1, child Safe as owner) upgrades the child first using SafeMigration.migrateWithFallbackHandler (or re-creates it as a 1.5.0 Safe). From then on every parent transaction that relies on the child's ERC-1271 signature reverts with empty data (parent bubbles the child's empty revert). If the child is the only owner above threshold, the parent can only proceed via the on-chain approveHash path until it is migrated. Reproduced with a temporary hardhat spec (deleted).
findings.evidence: CompatibilityFallbackHandler.sol:73 `function isValidSignature(bytes32 _dataHash, bytes calldata _signature)` is the only ERC-1271 entry point (bytecode scan: compatibilityFallbackHandler141 contains 0x20c13b0b, the 1.5.0 artifact does not). CHANGELOG.md:109-111 '#### Use the updated EIP-1271 function signature ... the legacy function was removed from the compatibility fallback handler contract.' SafeMigration.sol:71-74 migrateSingleton keeps the fallback handler slot (test/libraries/SafeMigration.spec.ts asserts FALLBACK_HANDLER_STORAGE_SLOT unchanged); :80-83 migrateWithFallbackHandler sets SAFE_FALLBACK_HANDLER (1.5.0 CFH). result.ruled_out: (1) 1.4.1 CFH on a 1.5.0 Safe, v==1 approved-hash shortcut: the 1.4.1 handler calls the legacy `checkSignatures(bytes32,bytes,bytes)` (Safe.sol:439-442), which forwards `msg.sender` = the handler address as executor. With r = handler address, `executor == currentOwner` skips the GS025 check but the owner-membership check (Safe.sol:409 `owners[currentOwner] == address(0)` -> GS026) rejects it because the handler is not an owner (empirically 'ecdsa1 + v1(r=handler): REVERT(GS026)'). For any real owner, v==1 requires an on-chain approveHash regardless of the dApp-side caller ('v1(r=user2) from user2, no approve: GS025'; 'v1(r=user3) from user3: GS025'; after approveHash: OK), which is identical to 1.3.0/1.4.1 semantics. A non-owner cannot obtain any shortcut. Only if owners deliberately add the handler itself as an owner would a 65-byte {handler,0,1} signature validate any hash — absurd self-inflicted misconfiguration, identical in 1.4.1, not reported. The direct-call caveat (owner calling the legacy overload gets a free pre-approval) is documented at Safe.sol:426 and reproduced ('direct legacy checkSignatures from owner user1 ... OK' vs 'from non-owner user3: GS025'). (2) Silent wrong data: no function in any mixed combination returned incorrect data; getMessageHash/getMessageHashForSafe/getModules/simulate/encodeTransactionData all matched off-chain expectations where they did not revert. The only failure mode is a revert (fails closed). (3) Signature forgery via the fallback re-entry: when the 1.5.0 handler's unknown selector 0xf855438b re-enters the old Safe's fallback and comes back to the handler with the Safe address appended, the CFH has no matching function and no fallback (empty revert); the EFH's catch-all fallback (FallbackHandler.sol:31-41) requires a safeMethods entry for that selector, which only the Safe itself (onlySelf) can register — so no untrusted party can hijack the path; a Safe could even register a legitimate shim for it, which is a workaround not a vulnerability. (4) ExtensibleFallbackHandler domain-verifier path on old Safes: it never calls checkSignatures, so a registered ISafeSignatureVerifier would still work on 1.3.0/1.4.1; only the default path breaks — consistent with the main finding, no separate issue. (5) SignMessageLib 1.5.0 on 1.3.0/1.4.1 Safes: uses only domainSeparator() (present since 1.3.0) and the same storage layout; empirically the signedMessages path worked on every version. (6) FallbackManager.setFallbackHandler lacking a version check is by design (handler is owner-trusted, documented at docs/overview.md:155-157); reported only as the missing-documentation aspect of finding 1, not as a code defect. findings.title: Out-of-range Enum.Operation is rejected only lazily in the canonical 0.7.6 build, via compiler-inserted INVALID (burns all gas, empty return data); the 0.8 build rejects at decode with an empty revert. No execution/guard bypass exists in either build.
findings.description: The task premise ("the legacy ABI decoder does NOT range-check Enum.Operation") is correct for the decoder but its implied conclusion (op>=2 continues as CALL) is wrong. With solc 0.7.6 / ABI coder v1 an enum parameter is decoded as its encodingType uint8 (value is masked with 0xff, no range check), so `getTransactionHash` (pure assembly, `mstore(add(ptr, 128), operation)` at contracts/Safe.sol:529) and `checkSignatures` accept op=2/255 and a correctly signed op=2 transaction passes the signature check. However, every Solidity-level use of the enum value carries a compiler-inserted range check that executes `INVALID` (0xfe): (a) `operation == Enum.Operation.DelegateCall` at contracts/base/Executor.sol:29; (b) ABI-encoding the enum for the `ITransactionGuard.checkTransaction` call at contracts/Safe.sol:175 and for `IModuleGuard.checkModuleTransaction` at contracts/base/ModuleManager.sol:120; (c) the SafeL2 events at contracts/SafeL2.sol:76 (`emit SafeMultiSigTransaction`) and :95 (`emit SafeModuleTransaction`); (d) `abi.encode(... operation ...)` in CompatibilityFallbackHandler.encodeTransactionData (contracts/handler/CompatibilityFallbackHandler.sol:218). Consequently op>=2 never reaches `call`/`delegatecall` on any path (execTransaction, execTransactionFromModule[ReturnData], SimulateTxAccessor.simulate), no component treats op!=Call as DelegateCall, and a 0.8-compiled guard installed on a 0.7.6 Safe is never even called with op>=2 (the Safe traps while encoding the call). The only observable consequences are: INVALID consumes all gas of the singleton frame (PoC: execTransaction(op=2) with gasLimit 1,000,000 -> status 0, gasUsed 984,863, i.e. everything except the 1/64 retained by the proxy frame; the same call on the 0.8.26 build costs 29,808 gas), the revert carries no data (no GS code; docs/error_codes.md has no entry), and the order of rejection differs by build (L1 Safe: after nonce++/checkSignatures/GS010 at Executor.sol:29, or at Safe.sol:175 if a guard is set; SafeL2: at SafeL2.sol:76 before hashing; 0.8.x: at calldata decode, before onBeforeExecTransaction). Note that the 0.8 decoder rejects with `revert(0,0)` (validator_revert), not Panic(0x21); Panic 0x21 only arises from explicit `Operation(x)` conversions (PoC confirmed both). The existing test test/core/Safe.Execution.spec.ts:184 ("should revert on unknown operation") passes because of the Executor.sol:29 INVALID, not because of decoder validation; it only asserts `.to.be.reverted`.
findings.attack_path: None. `operation` is always either owner-signed (execTransaction) or chosen by a trusted module/caller; an attacker cannot make a third party pay. A submitter/relayer that sends a signed op>=2 transaction burns its own gas limit (eth_estimateGas fails first), and a module forwarding an untrusted operation value loses 63/64 of its forwarded gas in its own frame. No state is changed (nonce unchanged, verified).

With DelegateCallTransactionGuard (0.7.6) or a solc-0.8.26 guard installed on Safe(L1): `invalid opcode at Safe.execTransaction (contracts/Safe.sol:175)`; module path: `at Safe.preModuleExecution (contracts/base/ModuleManager.sol:120)`; SafeL2 module path: `at SafeL2.onBeforeExecTransactionFromModule (contracts/SafeL2.sol:95)`. If a clean failure is wanted without bytecode growth concerns, read the raw word in assembly at the top of execTransaction/preModuleExecution (`uint256 raw; assembly { raw := operation }`, since `uint8(operation)` itself triggers the INVALID check in 0.7.6) and `revertWithError("GS0xx")` when raw > 1, then add the code to docs/error_codes.md. Strengthen test/core/Safe.Execution.spec.ts:184 to assert empty revert data and an unchanged nonce so a future compiler/coder change that silently accepts op>=2 (e.g. executing it as CALL) would be caught.

findings.description: The `benchmarks` job (.github/workflows/ci.yml:62-84) is the only place solc 0.8.24 is used (matrix at :67, settings `{"viaIR":false,"optimizer":{"enabled":true,"runs":1000000}}` at :70) and it runs just `npm run codesize` and `npm run benchmark` (:84), where package.json:27 defines `benchmark` as `hardhat test benchmark/*.ts`. No negative test, no signature-encoding edge case (contract signatures, secp256r1, approved hashes), no module/guard/fallback-handler/migration/EIP-7702 test runs on the 0.8 build (`npm run test`, package.json:20, is only run in the `tests` and `coverage` jobs with the default 0.7.6). The statement that "0.8.x builds are also tested" is therefore overstated: they are compiled and smoke-benchmarked. This matters because the two builds do not behave identically, as this lens shows: out-of-range `Enum.Operation` is rejected at ABI decode with an empty revert under 0.8 (ABI coder v2) but only at first use via INVALID under 0.7.6; raw calldata words with dirty high bits (e.g. 0x101) are rejected under 0.8 but masked to uint8 and executed under 0.7.6; the 0.8 matrix also uses optimizer runs=1000000 while the canonical build is unoptimized, so the 0.8 CI run does not validate the settings anyone would deploy with. Since all production deployments use the 0.7.6 artifacts, this is a process/robustness gap rather than an exploitable issue.
findings.attack_path: None directly. Risk is latent: a regression that only manifests under 0.8.x semantics (checked arithmetic, coder-v2 validation, different memory allocation) would not be caught by CI even though the pragma `>=0.7.0 <0.9.0` and the SOLIDITY_VERSION/SOLIDITY_SETTINGS escape hatches (hardhat.config.ts, .env.sample:15 suggests '0.8.19') invite third parties to compile and deploy 0.8 builds.

findings.title: getTransactionHash and the TypeScript signing helpers accept any uint8 operation (and the 0.7.6 build masks dirty high bits of the raw calldata word), so owners can be asked to sign well-formed but never-executable transactions
findings.description: `getTransactionHash` reads `operation` straight into the EIP-712 struct in assembly (contracts/Safe.sol:529, with the explicit warning at :496 that dirty bits are not cleaned). Under the 0.7.6 legacy decoder the parameter is already masked to uint8, so (verified) raw operation words 0x100, 0x101, 0x102, (1<<255)|1 and 0xff01 hash exactly as operation 0, 1, 2, 1 and 1, and a signature over operation=1 executes a calldata whose operation word is 0x101 as a DELEGATECALL (SafeMultiSigTransaction.operation = 1). The TS reference (src/utils/execution.ts:14,19 `uint8 operation`; buildSafeTransaction at :276 accepts any number) and `calculateSafeTransactionHash` produce the identical hash for operation 2 or 255, and the on-chain `checkSignatures` validates such signatures, although no such transaction can ever execute (finding 1). Because the hash binds the operation value and the nonce is not consumed, a signature over op>=2 cannot be replayed as op 0/1, so there is no security impact; the only effects are wasted signatures/relayer gas and a build-dependent divergence for calldata-based decoders: ethers v6 (verified) masks 0x101 to 1 like the 0.7.6 build, whereas strict decoders that validate padding bytes reject the calldata, and the 0.8 build rejects it on-chain. SafeL2 events and guard/module-guard arguments never carry out-of-range values (the Safe traps first), so event-based indexers are unaffected.
findings.attack_path: None with security impact: a malicious transaction proposer could get owners to sign an op>=2 transaction, but it can only ever fail (INVALID / decoder revert) and leaves no state change; a submitter can encode a signed op 0/1 transaction with dirty high bits in the operation word, but the executed semantics equal the signed semantics.
findings.evidence: PoC test B (scratchpad gap1_enum_operation.spec.ts): `getTransactionHash: raw words 0x100/0x101/0x102/(1<<255|1)/0xff01 hash as operation = word & 0xff`; `raw word 0x101 + sig over op=1 -> executed as DELEGATECALL, event op=1; ethers v6 decodeFunctionData => 1`; `raw word 0x100 + sig over op=0 -> executed as CALL, event op=0`. PoC test A: op=2/255 on-chain hash == calculateSafeTransactionHash and checkSignatures passes. 0.8.26 build: same raw word 0x101 calldata -> empty revert at decode.
findings.recommendation: Validate `operation` in the off-chain helpers (`buildSafeTransaction`/`safeSignTypedData` in src/utils/execution.ts should reject anything other than 0 or 1) and mention in docs/overview.md:88 / docs/signatures.md that only 0 and 1 are executable. On-chain, the assembly-level `raw > 1` check suggested in finding 1 would also make the hash function and the build-independent calldata semantics explicit.

findings.title: secp256r1 (v == 2) owners silently make a Safe's liveness depend on a chain-level precompile; no on-chain check and no owner-management/CHANGELOG warning, so counterfactual multi-chain Safes can be locked (funds stuck) on chains without 0x100
findings.description: OwnerManager.requireIsValidOwner (contracts/base/OwnerManager.sol:118-122) rejects only address(0), SENTINEL and the Safe itself, so a P-256-derived owner address (keccak256(qx||qy)[12:], computed at contracts/Safe.sol:393) is accepted by setupOwners/addOwnerWithThreshold/swapOwner on every chain. Such an owner can only ever authorize through the v == 2 branch (contracts/Safe.sol:354-396), which calls EIP7951.p256Verify; that function is defined to return false when the staticcall to 0x100 returns anything other than exactly one 32-byte word equal to 1 (contracts/common/EIP7951.sol:39-44, with the comment at :42-43 explicitly noting that an unsupported precompile yields returndatasize 0 and therefore false), after which checkNSignatures reverts GS028 (contracts/Safe.sol:396). The other signature types are unusable for that owner: v == 1 needs msg.sender == owner or approveHash by the owner (contracts/Safe.sol:353; approveHash is owner-only, GS030) and nobody holds a secp256k1 key for a keccak(qx||qy) address; v == 0 needs code at the owner address (SecuredSignatureValidator -> GS024); ecrecover cannot yield it. All owner-management functions are `authorized` (contracts/common/SelfAuthorized.sol:15-17, GS031) and therefore reachable only via execTransaction (which calls checkSignatures) or an enabled module. Consequently a Safe whose threshold cannot be met without P-256 owners (1-of-1 P-256, or n-of-n with any P-256 owner) and with no module is permanently inert on any chain where 0x100 is not a P-256 precompile: the owners cannot even swap themselves out or lower the threshold. Because SafeProxyFactory.createProxyWithNonce derives the CREATE2 salt from keccak256(initializer) and saltNonce only (contracts/proxies/SafeProxyFactory.sol:87-92) and SafeToL2Setup exists precisely so the same initializer yields the same address on every network (contracts/libraries/SafeToL2Setup.sol:7-9, 63-68), the P-256 owner list is baked into a chain-agnostic counterfactual address; assets sent to that address on a chain that lacks the precompile (or a chain that adopts it later) are frozen until that chain ships RIP-7212/EIP-7951. Nothing in the repository warns integrators at the owner-management layer: IOwnerManager.sol carries a prominent lock-out warning for the analogous 'Safe is its own owner' n/n case (contracts/interfaces/IOwnerManager.sol:30-36 and :58-64) but says nothing about P-256 owners; CHANGELOG.md contains no secp256r1/EIP-7951 entry at all (grep for secp256r1|7951|7212|1061 returns nothing); docs/overview.md and docs/signatures.md do not mention the feature; the only hint is the reactive debug tip under GS028 in docs/error_codes.md:53-55 ('Ensure ... either RIP-7212 or EIP-7951 is supported on the chain'). Note this is a liveness issue only: on a chain without the precompile no third party can use the P-256 owner slot either (every path above reverts), so it is not an asset-theft vector.
findings.attack_path: Not an attack; a user-foot-gun / robustness path. (1) User creates a Safe via createProxyWithNonce with owners = [P-256 address] and threshold 1 (or n-of-n including a P-256 owner), no module, on a chain that has 0x100 (e.g. an OP-Stack chain post-Fjord). (2) The identical counterfactual address is advertised/used on other chains; a counterparty sends tokens/ETH to it on a chain where 0x100 is not a P-256 precompile (or the Safe is deployed there via replayed initializer). (3) Every execTransaction on that chain reverts GS028 at contracts/Safe.sol:396 because p256Verify returns false (contracts/common/EIP7951.sol:44); approveHash reverts GS030; owner management is unreachable (GS031). Funds remain stuck until the chain ships the precompile. Reproduced with a temporary Hardhat spec (deleted): with HARDHAT_SECP256R1_PRECOMPILE unset, a 1-of-1 P-256 Safe's execTransaction(swapOwner(SENTINEL, p256Owner, eoa)) reverted with GS028 and approveHash with GS030; with HARDHAT_SECP256R1_PRECOMPILE=1 the same transaction succeeded and the owner was swapped.
findings.evidence: contracts/base/OwnerManager.sol:118-122 `if (owner == address(0) || owner == SENTINEL_OWNERS || (owner == address(this) && !isThisDelegatedAccount())) revertWithError("GS203");` (no other validation); contracts/Safe.sol:396 `if (currentOwner != signerAddress || !p256Verify(dataHash, r, s, qx, qy)) revertWithError("GS028");`; contracts/common/EIP7951.sol:39 `result := staticcall(gas(), 0x100, ptr, 0xa0, 0x00, 0x20)` and :44 `result := and(result, and(eq(returndatasize(), 0x20), eq(mload(0x00), 1)))`, comment :42-43 'in case the precompile is not supported, the returndatasize will be 0 making result false'; contracts/common/SelfAuthorized.sol:16 `if (msg.sender != address(this)) revertWithError("GS031");`; contracts/proxies/SafeProxyFactory.sol:89 `bytes32 salt = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(keccak256(initializer), saltNonce));`; contracts/libraries/SafeToL2Setup.sol:7-8 'facilitates the deployment of a Safe to the same address on all networks'; contracts/interfaces/IOwnerManager.sol:30-36 self-owner n/n lock-out warning with no P-256 counterpart; docs/error_codes.md:53-55 GS028 entry is the only mention; CHANGELOG.md has no secp256r1 entry. Hardhat PoC output: 'precompile absent: execTransaction(swapOwner) reverts GS028; Safe is locked' / 'precompile present: P-256 owner swapped itself out OK'.
findings.recommendation: Document the dependency where owners are configured, mirroring the existing self-owner warning: add a NatSpec warning to IOwnerManager.addOwnerWithThreshold/swapOwner (and ISafe.setup / docs/overview.md) that an owner address derived from a secp256r1 key can only sign where a RIP-7212/EIP-7951 precompile exists at 0x100, that a threshold reachable only through such owners (and no module) renders the Safe unusable on chains without it, and that counterfactual same-address deployments (createProxyWithNonce + SafeToL2Setup) therefore should either keep a secp256k1/contract owner within threshold reach, enable a recovery module, or use createChainSpecificProxyWithNonce. Add a CHANGELOG entry for #1061 stating the precompile requirement and the fact that an absent precompile is indistinguishable from an invalid signature (both yield GS028, by RIP-7212/EIP-7951 return convention). Optionally expose a view helper (or an off-chain check in the SDK) that probes 0x100 with a known-good vector before adding P-256 owners.

findings.title: EIP7951.p256Verify strict return-data check is only exercised against the EDR emulation (empty return on failure, RIP-7212 gas); the 32-byte-zero convention of early RIP-7212 deployments, over-long returns and a reverting 0x100 are untested although the code handles them
findings.description: The correctness of the v == 2 path across precompile variants rests on the single line contracts/common/EIP7951.sol:44 (`eq(returndatasize(), 0x20)` and `eq(mload(0x00), 1)`). RIP-7212 (final text) specifies 32-byte 1 on success and 'does not return any output data' on failure; EIP-7951 (Final) specifies 32-byte 1 / 0 bytes and states 'Same return values'. However the pre-April-2024 RIP-7212 text and implementations derived from it (zkSync Era's original P256Verify, Daimo's verifier) returned a 32-byte zero word on failure, so both conventions exist in the wild. The repository's @secp256r1 tests (test/core/Safe.Signatures.spec.ts:580-717) run only against Hardhat/EDR's `enableRip7212` (hardhat.config.ts:120), which I measured to return empty bytes on failure, 32-byte 1 on success, to charge 3450 gas (RIP-7212 value, address treated as warm) and to accept high-s signatures. No test pins the behaviour for a 32-byte-zero return, a >32-byte return, a word != 1, or a reverting 0x100. I verified with hardhat_setCode mocks at 0x100 (temporary spec, deleted) that the Safe reverts GS028 in all four cases and that the check does not propagate a revert from 0x100, so there is no defect, but the guarantee is unpinned by the suite. The same mock also demonstrates the trust assumption: code at 0x100 that returns 1 unconditionally makes any (r,s) valid for a registered P-256 owner.
findings.attack_path: None (test-coverage gap). A future refactor of the assembly in EIP7951.p256Verify (e.g. dropping the returndatasize check or using abi.decode) would not be caught by CI for the 32-byte-zero / over-long / revert cases, because EDR never produces them.
findings.evidence: contracts/common/EIP7951.sol:44 `result := and(result, and(eq(returndatasize(), 0x20), eq(mload(0x00), 1)))`; test/core/Safe.Signatures.spec.ts:541-578 (negative test without precompile, runs in test:hardhat/test:L2), :580-615 (positive, @secp256r1), :617-640 (GS021/GS027 encoding), :642-677 (wrong signer), :679-717 (bad r) -- all through EDR only; package.json:24 `"test:secp256r1": "HARDHAT_SECP256R1_PRECOMPILE=1 hardhat test --grep '@secp256r1'"`; hardhat.config.ts:120 `enableRip7212: HARDHAT_SECP256R1_PRECOMPILE === "1"`. Measured via wrapper contract: enableRip7212=true valid -> returndatasize=32 word=1, gasUsedByStaticcall=3813; invalid -> returndatasize=0, 3743; enableRip7212=false -> returndatasize=0, 2793 (cold account). Mock results: 32-byte zero -> GS028; 64-byte return with word==1 -> GS028; word==2 -> GS028; REVERT -> GS028; always-1 code -> forged (0,0) signature accepted.
findings.recommendation: Add tests that install mock code at 0x100 with hardhat_setCode (works when HARDHAT_SECP256R1_PRECOMPILE is unset) covering: 32-byte zero on failure (old RIP-7212/zkSync/Daimo convention) -> GS028; 64-byte return starting with 1 -> GS028; 32-byte word != 1 -> GS028; reverting 0x100 -> GS028 with no revert propagation; and a 32-byte 1 -> success, to pin the strict decoding independent of EDR's emulation. Optionally also run the @secp256r1 cases in the coverage job (it currently runs without the flag so they are skipped).

result.ruled_out: (A) exploitability: on a chain without 0x100 the P-256 owner slot cannot be abused by anyone (v==2 -> GS028, v==1 needs the owner as msg.sender/approveHash which no one controls, v==0 needs code at the owner address -> GS024, ecrecover cannot produce a keccak(qx||qy) address); it is purely a liveness loss, reported as low. EIP-7702 delegated accounts are not affected because the EOA can call the `authorized` functions directly (msg.sender == address(this)). Safes with a module or with secp256k1/contract owners within threshold reach are not locked. (B) Return-convention variance: `eq(returndatasize(),0x20) && mload(0)==1` is correct for both documented conventions (empty on failure per final RIP-7212 and EIP-7951; 32-byte zero per the pre-April-2024 RIP-7212 text used by early zkSync/Daimo) and I confirmed by mock that over-long returns, word!=1 and reverts all yield GS028 with no revert propagation; scratch-space reuse at 0x00 is safe because stale memory is only consulted when returndatasize==32 (i.e. after it was overwritten). Laxness: an owner-address binding does NOT protect against a psychic-signature-style precompile (one accepting r=s=0 for any key), so laxness would matter in principle; however both RIP-7212 and EIP-7951 mandate 0<r,s<n and on-curve/non-infinity checks, all geth-derived implementations (bor, op-geth, nitro, bsc-geth) share geth's secp256r1.Verify with those checks, EDR rejected r=s=0, off-curve, (0,0) and bad lengths, and I could not probe live chains (proxy blocked), so no concrete chain-specific deviation was found and nothing is reported. The EIP-7951-noted RIP-7212 omissions (R' at infinity; r' ≡ r mod n) are not forgeable without the private key (infinity requires r ≡ -h/d mod n) and the mod-n comparison can only reject, with probability ~2^-128, a valid signature. High-s acceptance (malleability) is confirmed and explicitly documented at contracts/Safe.sol:359-360. (C) No chain hosting a different precompile at 0x100 was identified: OP-Stack (Fjord+), Arbitrum (ArbOS 31+), Polygon PoS (PIP-27), zkSync Era, Monad, Sei/Cosmos-EVM, Ethereum (Fusaka/EIP-7951) all use 0x100 for P256VERIFY; other chains' custom precompiles live elsewhere (Arbitrum 0x64-0x6f/0xff, Celo 0xf3-0xff, Moonbeam 0x800+, Rootstock 0x01000006+, Avalanche 0x0100000000000000000000000000000000000000-range). Code can only be placed at 0x100 by genesis/protocol action (no CREATE/CREATE2/7702 path), so the 'always-1 at 0x100' mock is a protocol-trust assumption, not an attack. The Polygon PoS 'invalid returns empty' behaviour that triggered the RIP-7212 spec change is now the spec and is handled. (D) Gas: EIP7951.sol:39 forwards gas() so the 3450 (RIP-7212) vs 6900 (EIP-7951) vs 12000 (zkSync) difference only changes gas estimation; an under-gassed STATICCALL returns 0 -> GS028 (never a false accept); the GS010 check runs after checkSignatures so precompile gas is already accounted for; the hardhat flag name `enableRip7212` and EDR's 3450/warm accounting mean local benchmarks understate mainnet cost (estimation only, not reported). The EIP-7623 calldata floor masks precompile gas in eth_estimateGas for direct calls (observed), irrelevant to the Safe. Tests: `npm run test` (package.json:20) does run test:secp256r1 (package.json:24) in CI (ci.yml:42); a 'precompile absent' negative test exists (Safe.Signatures.spec.ts:541-578, untagged, runs under test:hardhat and test:L2 where enableRip7212 is false) and asserts GS028; the only gaps are the mock-convention cases listed in the informational finding and the coverage job skipping @secp256r1 cases. Encoding/bounds: GS021/GS027 checks at Safe.sol:367-368 use SafeMath and are covered at spec :617-640; `uint256(s).add(128) > signatures.length` correctly bounds the 128-byte dynamic part. CHANGELOG 'Expected addresses' staleness relative to post-#1061 bytecode is subsumed by the already-confirmed 'post-audit changes absent from CHANGELOG' finding and is outside this lens. Nothing in contracts/test/** affects production deployments for this lens.

verdict.reasoning:
Every factual claim in G3-1 checks out against the code (contracts unchanged since f8fc2f2; the extra local commits only add test scaffolding):
- contracts/base/OwnerManager.sol:118-122 `requireIsValidOwner` rejects only address(0), SENTINEL_OWNERS and address(this) (unless EIP-7702-delegated). A keccak(qx||qy)-derived address is a plain 20-byte value the contract cannot distinguish from an EOA, so no on-chain P-256-awareness is possible at owner-add time.
- contracts/Safe.sol:354-396: the v==2 branch computes `signerAddress := keccak256(add(sig,0x40),0x40)` and reverts `GS028` at :396 if `!p256Verify(...)`.
- contracts/common/EIP7951.sol:39 `staticcall(gas(), 0x100, ptr, 0xa0, 0x00, 0x20)` and :44 `result := and(result, and(eq(returndatasize(), 0x20), eq(mload(0x00), 1)))`; comment at :42-43 explicitly says an unsupported precompile yields returndatasize 0 => false. So an absent precompile is indistinguishable from an invalid signature (both GS028), by the EIP-7951/RIP-7212 return convention.
- contracts/Safe.sol:447-448 `approveHash` reverts GS030 for non-owners; contracts/common/SelfAuthorized.sol:16 GS031 makes all owner-management functions reachable only via execTransaction/modules. No other signature type can authorize for a P-256 address (v==0 needs code at the address -> GS024 via SecuredSignatureValidator; ecrecover cannot yield keccak(qx||qy)).
- contracts/proxies/SafeProxyFactory.sol:89 derives the CREATE2 salt from keccak256(initializer)+saltNonce; contracts/libraries/SafeToL2Setup.sol:7-8 exists for same-address-on-all-networks deployment. So the owner list is baked into a chain-agnostic address.
- Documentation state: contracts/interfaces/IOwnerManager.sol:30-36 and :58-64 carry the self-owner n/n lock-out warning; nothing analogous for P-256 owners in IOwnerManager/ISafe/docs/overview.md/docs/signatures.md. CHANGELOG.md's "Version 1.5.0 / Changes" section lists 13+ feature entries and the "Current version" section lists only #1115; neither mentions secp256r1/EIP-7951/#1061. docs/error_codes.md:53-55 (GS028) is the only place that states the precompile requirement ("Ensure ... either RIP-7212 or EIP-7951 is supported on the chain").

Why informational rather than low: (1) There is no code defect — the behavior is exactly the designed EIP-7951 semantics and is explicitly tested by test/core/Safe.Signatures.spec.ts:541-578 ("should revert when RIP-7212/RIP-7951 is not enabled" asserts GS028 with `HARDHAT_SECP256R1_PRECOMPILE` unset), so the maintainers are aware of it. (2) No on-chain mitigation is feasible: the contract cannot tell an address is P-256-derived, and probing 0x100 at owner-add time would break counterfactual deployments and chains that adopt the precompile later. (3) Under Safe's threat model, owner/configuration choices are the owners' responsibility, and this is the same accepted class of self-inflicted lock-out as adding an ERC-1271 contract owner that is not deployed on another chain (e.g. a passkey signer contract or a Safe-as-owner), or adding an address whose key is lost; the only such case with a NatSpec warning (self-as-owner) is called out because the contract contains an explicit carve-out for it. (4) The lock is bounded ("until the chain ships the precompile"); EIP-7951 shipped on Ethereum mainnet in Fusaka and RIP-7212 is live on the major OP-Stack/Arbitrum/Polygon/zkSync chains, so the affected chain set is small and shrinking. (5) It is not an asset-theft vector: on a chain without the precompile no third party can use the P-256 owner slot either. Net: an accurate, actionable documentation/UX recommendation — the category a Certora/Ackee-style report files as Informational.

Side note for the orchestrator: #1061 (EIP-7951 signer) landed 2026-01-14, after BOTH audited commits in docs/audit_1_5_0.md (Certora 1c8b24a = 2025-01-23, Ackee 5d26505 = 2025-05-27), so the v==2 branch in Safe.sol:354-396 and contracts/common/EIP7951.sol are post-audit code in the same sense as #1115/#1123 and deserve the same scrutiny. I could not confirm whether the deployed v1.5.0 singleton contains the v==2 branch (no local tags; upstream GitHub access not enabled for this session), which only affects which CHANGELOG section the omission belongs in.
verdict.preconditions: Entirely self-inflicted configuration, no attacker required: (a) a Safe whose threshold cannot be reached without P-256 (v==2) owners — e.g. 1-of-1 with a keccak(qx||qy)-derived owner, or any n-of-n / threshold > number of non-P-256 owners; (b) no enabled module (ModuleManager path bypasses checkSignatures); (c) the Safe is deployed, or holds funds at its counterfactual createProxyWithNonce address, on a chain where address 0x100 is not a RIP-7212/EIP-7951 P-256 precompile (or where it is adopted only later). Under these conditions execTransaction always reverts GS028 (Safe.sol:396 via EIP7951.sol:44), approveHash reverts GS030 (Safe.sol:448), and owner management is unreachable (SelfAuthorized.sol:16, GS031), so funds/control are inert until that chain ships the precompile. Also relevant: any contract (v==0) owner not deployed on the target chain produces the identical cross-chain lock-out, which is already an accepted design property.
verdict.exploit_sketch: Not an attack path; a user foot-gun. (1) Deploy via SafeProxyFactory.createProxyWithNonce (salt = keccak256(keccak256(initializer), saltNonce), SafeProxyFactory.sol:89), optionally through SafeToL2Setup, with owners=[P-256 address], threshold=1, no module, on a chain that has 0x100. (2) Advertise the chain-agnostic address; a counterparty sends assets to it on a chain lacking the precompile, or the initializer is replayed there. (3) On that chain: every execTransaction -> checkNSignatures v==2 branch -> p256Verify staticcall returns no data -> GS028; approveHash from any EOA -> GS030; addOwnerWithThreshold/swapOwner/changeThreshold/enableModule -> GS031 unless via execTransaction. No recovery until the chain adopts RIP-7212/EIP-7951. No third party gains anything on either chain.

verdict.reasoning:
The finder's facts check out, but they describe a test-coverage gap, not a security or correctness defect, so under the impact lens this is not a real finding (confidence that it is an exploitable/correctness defect: ~0.1; confidence in this characterisation itself: ~0.95).

What I verified in the code:
- /home/user/safe-smart-account/contracts/common/EIP7951.sol:39 `result := staticcall(gas(), 0x100, ptr, 0xa0, 0x00, 0x20)` and :44 `result := and(result, and(eq(returndatasize(), 0x20), eq(mload(0x00), 1)))`. This requires success AND exactly 32 bytes of return data AND the word == 1. Because `staticcall` never propagates a callee revert, a reverting 0x100 just yields result=0; a 0-byte return fails the returndatasize test (so stale scratch-space contents at 0x00 are irrelevant); a >32-byte return fails the size test even though only the first 32 bytes are copied; a 32-byte zero / 2 / left-aligned 0x01 fails the word test. This is the strictest possible decoding and is correct for both the RIP-7212 (empty on failure) and the older 32-byte-zero convention.
- /home/user/safe-smart-account/contracts/Safe.sol:354-396: v==2 path binds the owner to keccak256(qx,qy) (:393) and reverts GS028 if `currentOwner != signerAddress || !p256Verify(...)` (:396), so a bogus precompile result can only matter for an address that is already a registered P-256 owner.
- Existing tests: /home/user/safe-smart-account/test/core/Safe.Signatures.spec.ts:537-539 gates on `enableRip7212`; :541-578 (no-precompile -> GS028), :580-615 (positive), :617-640 (GS021/GS027), :642-677 (wrong signer), :679-717 (bad r) run only against EDR's emulation (hardhat.config.ts:120 `enableRip7212: HARDHAT_SECP256R1_PRECOMPILE === "1"`; package.json:24 `test:secp256r1`). The CI coverage job (.github/workflows/ci.yml:44-60) runs `npm run coverage` without the flag, so the positive and bad-r cases are skipped there.
- Certora summarises the function away: /home/user/safe-smart-account/certora/specs/Signatures.spec:17 `function EIP7951.p256Verify(...) internal returns (bool) => CONSTANT;`, so formal verification does not cover the assembly either.
- Timeline: P-256 support landed in 0e91d99 "Add EIP-7951 Signer Support (#1061)" on 2026-01-14, after the v1.5.0 audit reports (a1e7f4a 2025-02-18 Certora, a0f4c36 2025-06-10 Ackee); docs/ contain no audit mention of #1061/EIP-7951, and docs/signatures.md does not document signature type 2 at all (only docs/error_codes.md:50-55 mention GS027/GS028). So the only check on this assembly is the EDR-based test set -- which supports the finder's point that the strict decoding is unpinned, but still does not make it a defect.

What I ran (temporary spec test/_audit_tmp_G3-2.spec.ts, deleted afterwards; git status clean):
- Without the flag, hardhat_setCode mocks at 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000100 for a valid P-256 signature from a registered owner: 32-byte zero -> GS028; 64-byte return with first word 1 -> GS028; 32-byte word 2 -> GS028; 1-byte 0x01 -> GS028; left-aligned 0x01 in 32 bytes -> GS028; REVERT -> GS028 (no revert propagation); STOP/empty -> GS028; 32-byte 1 -> accepted. Always-1 code also accepts a forged (r,s)=(0,0) signature for a registered P-256 owner (trust assumption demonstration).
- With HARDHAT_SECP256R1_PRECOMPILE=1, raw eth_call to 0x100: valid -> 0x..01 (32 bytes); invalid -> 0x (0 bytes); short input -> 0x. Confirms EDR never produces the 32-byte-zero / over-long / revert shapes, so the existing suite cannot exercise those branches of the check.
- Existing @secp256r1 tests: 4 passing with the flag; with it off, 2 pass and 2 are skipped, as the finder said.

Impact assessment under Safe's threat model: no attack path exists. Code at 0x100 cannot be placed by an attacker (CREATE/CREATE2 addresses are hash-derived; only a chain upgrade can populate a precompile address), and trusting the chain's precompile is the same assumption as trusting ecrecover at 0x01; docs/error_codes.md:55 already tells integrators the chain must support RIP-7212/EIP-7951. A hypothetical non-conforming precompile that does not return a 32-byte 1 would only cause valid P-256 signatures to be rejected (GS028), i.e. a chain-specific liveness issue for P-256 owners rather than a loss of funds, and I know of no live 0x100 deployment with such a format. The finding therefore reduces to: (1) a recommendation to pin the strict return-data decoding with 0x100 mocks so a future refactor (e.g. switching to abi.decode or dropping the returndatasize check) is caught, and (2) a related documentation gap (signature type 2 absent from docs/signatures.md). Both are informational; neither is a security or correctness defect in the deployed code.
verdict.preconditions: For the only scenario with security impact (always-true code at 0x100 making any (r,s) valid for a registered P-256 owner): a chain-level upgrade or malicious/buggy precompile implementation at address 0x100 -- not reachable by any user, owner, module, or relayer under the Safe threat model, and equivalent in trust to ecrecover at 0x01. For the liveness scenario (valid signatures rejected with GS028): a chain whose 0x100 precompile does not return exactly a 32-byte 1 on success; no such live deployment is known (RIP-7212 and EIP-7951 both specify 32-byte 1 on success; the historical divergence between implementations concerns only the failure case, which the check handles correctly). For the test-coverage gap itself: no preconditions; it is simply that EDR's emulation never produces the 32-byte-zero / over-long / revert shapes, so CI cannot detect a future regression of EIP7951.sol:44.
verdict.exploit_sketch: None -- there is no exploit. Demonstration of the trust assumption only (run in a temporary Hardhat spec, now deleted): register owner = address(keccak256(qx,qy)) for a P-256 key with threshold 1; call checkSignatures(address,bytes32,bytes) with a v==2 signature whose (r,s)=(0,0): with no code at 0x100 -> GS028; after hardhat_setCode(0x100, 0x600160005260206000f3) (returns 32-byte 1 unconditionally) -> accepted. This requires replacing the chain's precompile and is not an attacker capability. Conversely, with mocks returning 32-byte zero (0x600060005260206000f3), 64 bytes starting with 1 (0x600160005260406000f3), word 2, 1-byte 0x01, left-aligned 0x01, REVERT (0x60006000fd) or STOP (0x00), a genuinely valid P-256 signature is rejected with GS028 and no revert is propagated, confirming the strict check at contracts/common/EIP7951.sol:44 behaves correctly for every return-data convention.
